make_flextable <- function(df) {
  ft <- flextable::flextable(df)
  ft <- flextable::autofit(ft)
  ft <- flextable::align(ft, align = "left", part = "all")

  if ("Parameter" %in% names(df)) {
    vals <- df$Parameter
    clean_label <- function(x) {
      x <- gsub("~", " ", x)
      x <- gsub("italic\\(([^)]+)\\)", "\\1", x)
      x <- gsub("\\s+", " ", x)
      trimws(x)
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Pop.~growth~rate~(italic(lambda))")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(
          "Pop. growth rate (", "λ", ")"
        )
      )
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Damping~ratio~(italic(rho))")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(
          "Damping ratio (", "ρ", ")"
        )
      )
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Repro.~value~(Veg.)")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph("Reproductive value (vegetative stage)")
      )
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Generation~time~(italic(T))")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(
          "Generation time (", flextable::as_i("T"), ")"
        )
      )
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Life~expectancy~(italic(l[0]))")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(
          "Life expectancy (", flextable::as_i("l"), flextable::as_sub("0"), ")"
        )
      )
    }

    idx_other <- setdiff(seq_along(vals), which(vals %in% c(
      "Pop.~growth~rate~(italic(lambda))",
      "Damping~ratio~(italic(rho))",
      "Repro.~value~(Veg.)",
      "Generation~time~(italic(T))",
      "Life~expectancy~(italic(l[0]))"
    )))
    if (length(idx_other) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx_other,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(clean_label(vals[idx_other]))
      )
    }
  }

  ft
}

fmt_mean_sd <- function(x, s, digits = 2) {
  paste0(formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f"), " ± ",
         formatC(s, digits = digits, format = "f"))
}

fmt_n_prop <- function(n, p, digits = 1) {
  paste0(n, " (", formatC(100 * p, digits = digits, format = "f"), "%)")
}

boundary_lookup <- function(category, column) {
  out <- boundary_smallN_group |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      group_value = dplyr::case_when(
        group_type == "Matrix dimension" & group_value == "3-5" ~ "3-5 stages",
        group_type == "Matrix dimension" & group_value == "6+" ~ "6+ stages",
        TRUE ~ group_value
      )
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(group_value == category) |>
    dplyr::pull({{ column }})
  out[[1]]
}

# Supplementary Methods

## S1.1 Sampling-distribution workflow used for each MPM

For each focal matrix population model (MPM), we reconstructed transition-level sampling distributions from reported transition counts (or equivalent sample-size information). We then generated 2,000 parametric bootstrap draws per MPM by sampling each transition from its likelihood (multinomial for survival/growth/retrogression transitions and Poisson for recruitment transitions), rebuilding the full MPM for each draw, and recalculating each derived demographic quantity from that draw. We treated structural zeros (biologically impossible transitions) as fixed zeros in all draws, and treated sampling zeros (possible but unobserved transitions) as uncertain parameters under the same likelihood models used for non-zero transitions. When a recovered stage-specific sample size was zero, we retained the published point-estimate transition column unchanged in all bootstrap draws rather than treating it as structurally fixed at zero; this preserves the published matrix while acknowledging that no additional sampling variance can be propagated for that column.

This produced a sampling distribution for each derived quantity used downstream (e.g. life expectancy, shape, log population growth rate). Point estimates in the manuscript correspond to values derived directly from the reported matrix entries; uncertainty-aware summaries correspond to moments of these bootstrap distributions.

## S1.2 Age-from-stage derivation, truncation, and shape metric

Life expectancy and shape were derived from survivorship trajectories obtained using age-from-stage methods, starting from the first reproductive stage. Shape was calculated using the pace-shape framework metric (Baudisch and Stott 2019). Because stage-based survivorship can converge to an artefactual mortality plateau, shape was calculated on truncated trajectories up to quasi-stable convergence (distance threshold 1%).

## S1.3 Pooled and mean MPM handling

Analysis 1 used one population-level MPM per population. Where a pooled population MPM was available, it was used; otherwise, a mean population MPM was used; if neither was available, a population-level matrix was constructed as the element-wise mean of the available annual individual MPMs. When COMPADRE included both site-specific population rows and aggregate rows that combined multiple populations, only the site-specific population rows were retained, so that each population contributed a single analysis unit. For uncertainty propagation in pooled or mean matrices, stage-specific sample sizes were pooled across years before bootstrap simulation. This captures within-year sampling variation but does not fully represent between-year process variation, so the resulting uncertainty should be interpreted conservatively.

## S1.4 Bayesian model priors and fitting settings

Stan models and priors are defined in `models/*.stan`. For the two main analyses:

- Analysis 1 models use weakly informative normal priors for location/slope terms and normal priors for scale terms (see `models/regress_hier.stan` and `models/regress_hier_error.stan`).
- Analysis 2 uses two models with Gaussian-process regression forms and normal priors on GP hyperparameters and coefficients (see `models/movbeta_gprc.stan` and `models/movbeta_gprc_err.stan`).
- Analysis 3 uses the same Gaussian-process recruitment model pair as analysis 2 (`models/movbeta_gprc.stan` and `models/movbeta_gprc_err.stan`) together with a simpler spring-temperature regression pair using weakly informative normal priors on regression coefficients and scale terms (`models/regress.stan` and `models/regress_log_err.stan`).

Fitting settings used in scripts:

- Analysis 1 (`scripts/S07_case_study_1_analysis.R`): `chains = 2`, `iter = 4000`, `warmup = 2000-3000`, `seed = 5654`.
- Analysis 2 (`scripts/S12_case_study_2.R`): `iter = 5000` for key models, `seed = 5654`, with additional control settings for GP fits.
- Analysis 3 (`scripts/S14_case_study_3_astragalus.R`): `iter = 5000`, `seed = 5654`, using the same GP control settings as analysis 2 for recruitment models and matched regression settings for the simplified spring-temperature models.

## S1.5 Variance-component summary (sampling-to-other ratio)

For each parameter, the total observed variance was partitioned into:

- sampling component: mean within-MPM sampling variance from bootstrap draws;
- residual component: remaining variance among populations/species.

The reported summary is Eq. \@ref(eq:var-ratio):

\begin{equation}
\text{ratio} = \frac{v_{\text{sampling}}}{v_{\text{residual}}}
(\#eq:var-ratio)
\end{equation}

Ratios above 1 indicate that sampling uncertainty exceeds residual biological variation for that parameter.

## S1.6 Simplified spring-temperature model (analysis 2)

In addition to the monthly-lagged GP model, we fit a simplified spring summary model with mean spring temperature deviation as the predictor, under both point-estimate and uncertainty-aware formulations. The contrasts reported in the manuscript use posterior medians and 95% interval widths from these paired models.

For the stage-specific survival panel in analysis 2 (Fig. 5C), we derived annual stage-specific survival as the column sums of the \(U\) matrix for each year and stage, then compared two logit-scale models per stage: (i) a stable-stage distribution (SSD)-weighted quasibinomial point-estimate model, \(\texttt{surv} \sim \texttt{tmp}\), where weights are the stable stage distribution from each annual \(U\) matrix; and (ii) a binomial count model, \(\texttt{cbind}(n_{\text{surv}}, n_{\text{fail}}) \sim \texttt{tmp}\), where \(n_{\text{surv}}\) and \(n_{\text{fail}}\) are survived and non-survived counts implied by stage sample size and \(U\)-column survival probability.

## S1.7 Reporting recommendations for future MPM studies

To support uncertainty propagation in secondary analyses, primary studies should report (at a minimum):

- transition-level sample sizes for each matrix element (or reconstructable transition count tables);
- clear identification of pooled/mean matrices and pooling rules;
- uncertainty estimates on model-appropriate scales (e.g. linear predictor where relevant);
- explicit projection interval, stage definitions, and treatment filters used to derive published matrices.

These items are usually sufficient for parametric uncertainty reconstruction in compiled databases.

## S1.8 Included versus excluded studies in the current target-study screen

To assess whether the studies retained for uncertainty analysis differed systematically from those screened but not retained, we compared the 23 post-2010 studies in the final dataset that still fall within the current reproducible COMPADRE screen against the remaining 69 screened studies. For each study, we summarized mean matrix dimension, mean stage-specific survival (the average of \(U\)-column survival probabilities across matrices), and the proportions of stage-specific survival estimates equal to 0, equal to 1, or at either boundary. Dominant life form was defined as the modal `OrganismType` among a study's matrices. Three additional post-2010 studies in the final dataset do not fall within the current screen under `r compadre_version_label` (`r paste(sprintf('*%s*', included_not_in_screen$SpeciesAccepted), collapse = ', ')`), and five further studies were pre-2010 additions; these eight studies were excluded from this screen-based comparison.

## S1.9 Study and species identities in analysis 1

Analysis 1 used a subset of the full compiled dataset: 68 population-level entries representing 25 species. Study-level and species-level identities (including COMPADRE `SpeciesAuthor` labels) are provided in Table S6.

## S1.10 Multi-site extension for analysis 3 (*Astragalus scaphoides*)

To evaluate whether inference robustness in analysis 2 generalised across populations, we repeated the same paired modelling framework for all available *Astragalus scaphoides* sites with sufficient annual coverage. For each site, we fit (i) a point-estimate model and (ii) a sampling-uncertainty model for recruitment-temperature relationships, using both the monthly-lag Gaussian-process specification and the simplified spring-temperature specification. We then compared posterior medians and 95% intervals between model formulations within site. This design isolates the contribution of uncertainty propagation while preserving site-specific ecological context.

For stage-specific survival in analysis 3, we used the same matched pair as in analysis 2: an SSD-weighted quasibinomial point-estimate model (\(\texttt{surv} \sim \texttt{tmp}\), weights from the stable stage distribution of each annual \(U\) matrix) and a binomial count model (\(\texttt{cbind}(n_{\text{surv}}, n_{\text{fail}}) \sim \texttt{tmp}\)). This keeps the linear predictor and response scale aligned across formulations, differing only in whether survival is treated as a plug-in proportion or as counts with explicit sampling uncertainty.

For sensitivity analyses intended to mimic database-only use (no access to true stage sample sizes), we re-fit stage-specific point-estimate models under two alternatives: (i) no weighting and (ii) SSD weighting derived from each annual \(U\) matrix.

## S1.11 Boundary survival estimates and small stage-specific sample sizes in analysis 1

To assess whether the conditions most likely to distort point estimates were concentrated in particular parts of the analysis 1 dataset, we summarized the 68 population-level entries with recovered stage counts by COMPADRE `OrganismType` (used here as the available life-form grouping) and by broad matrix-dimension class (3-5 versus 6+ stages). For each population-level matrix, we recorded whether any stage-specific survival estimate lay exactly on the boundary (0 or 1), whether any stage had \(N < 20\) or \(N < 50\), and the minimum stage-specific sample size. These summaries are descriptive and intended to identify where potentially fragile point estimates are concentrated in the analysed subset.

## S1.12 Displacement magnitude versus boundary survival structure

To quantify the mechanism behind point-estimate displacement in analysis 1, we compared each population-level point estimate to the median of its sampling distribution for mature life expectancy and shape. We defined displacement magnitude as the absolute difference between the point estimate and the sampling-distribution median; for life expectancy, this was calculated on the \(\log_{10}\) scale to reflect multiplicative discrepancies. We then related displacement magnitude to two predictors derived from the same population-level matrix: (i) the number of stage-specific survival estimates at the boundary (0 or 1), and (ii) the proportion of observed individuals belonging to boundary-survival stages, calculated from the recovered stage-specific sample sizes. We summarized these relationships with simple linear regressions and visualized them with scatter plots and fitted lines.

## S1.13 Sensitivity to the quasi-stable-distribution truncation threshold

To assess whether the shape metric was sensitive to the truncation rule used to avoid artefactual mortality plateaus, we repeated the analysis 1 shape calculation using quasi-stable-distribution convergence thresholds of 0.5% and 5%, alongside the 1% threshold used in the main analysis. For each population-level MPM that remained estimable under all three thresholds, we recalculated the point estimate of shape and the bootstrap sampling-distribution summary using the threshold-specific truncation age \(q\). We then compared the resulting shape estimates to the 1% baseline using pairwise correlations, absolute differences, sign changes around zero, and shifts in \(q\).

# Supplementary Results

## S2.1 Sensitivity to point-estimate weighting choice

Across estimable stages in analysis 2, switching from no weighting to SSD weighting changed temperature-coefficient medians by at most `r round(max(case2_stage_cmp$abs_beta_diff, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` on the logit scale, with interval widths changing by `r round(min(case2_stage_cmp$width_ssd - case2_stage_cmp$width_no, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` to `r round(max(case2_stage_cmp$width_ssd - case2_stage_cmp$width_no, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` (Table S9).

Across estimable site-stage combinations in analysis 3, the corresponding maximum absolute median shift was `r round(max(case3_stage_cmp$abs_beta_diff, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`, and interval-width differences ranged from `r round(min(case3_stage_cmp$width_ssd - case3_stage_cmp$width_no, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` to `r round(max(case3_stage_cmp$width_ssd - case3_stage_cmp$width_no, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` (Table S10). These sensitivity checks show how weighting assumptions alter point-estimate uncertainty when true stage sample sizes are unavailable.

## S2.2 Where do boundary estimates and small stage counts occur?

Among the `r boundary_smallN_overall$n_populations_with_counts` analysis 1 population-level entries with recovered stage counts, `r round(boundary_smallN_overall$pct_pop_with_any_boundary, 1)`% contained at least one boundary survival estimate and `r round(boundary_smallN_overall$pct_pop_with_any_small_n20, 1)`% contained at least one stage estimated from fewer than 20 individuals. These conditions tended to co-occur: the population-level proportion of boundary survival estimates was positively correlated with the proportion of stages having \(N < 20\) (\(r = `r round(boundary_smallN_overall$corr_prop_boundary_prop_small_n20, 2)`\)).

By life form, herbaceous perennials made up most of the analysed subset and showed the highest frequency among the well-represented categories, with `r herb_boundary_pct`% of entries containing at least one boundary survival estimate and `r herb_small20_pct`% containing at least one stage with \(N < 20\). Succulents showed lower corresponding values (`r succ_boundary_pct`% and `r succ_small20_pct`%, respectively). Woody life forms were too sparsely represented in the final subset for strong conclusions. By matrix dimension, both features were more common in 6+-stage matrices than in 3-5-stage matrices (`r dim6p_boundary_pct`% versus `r dim35_boundary_pct`% for any boundary estimate; `r dim6p_small20_pct`% versus `r dim35_small20_pct`% for any stage with \(N < 20\); Table S12).

## S2.3 Does displacement increase with boundary survival structure?

Displacement magnitude increased with both measures of boundary-survival structure (Figure S3; Table S13). For shape, the absolute difference between the point estimate and the sampling-distribution median increased with the number of boundary survival stages (slope = `r shape_nb_slope`, 95% CI `r shape_nb_ci`) and with the proportion of individuals in boundary-survival stages (slope = `r shape_pb_slope`, 95% CI `r shape_pb_ci`). For mature life expectancy, the same pattern was evident on the \(\log_{10}\) scale (number of boundary stages: slope = `r l0_nb_slope`, 95% CI `r l0_nb_ci`; proportion of individuals in boundary-survival stages: slope = `r l0_pb_slope`, 95% CI `r l0_pb_ci`). The fitted models explained a modest but non-trivial share of the among-matrix variation in displacement magnitude (\(R^2 = `r sprintf('%.3f', disp_r2_min)`-`r sprintf('%.3f', disp_r2_max)`\)). These results support the proposed mechanism: matrices with more boundary-survival structure tend to show larger mismatches between point estimates and the centres of their sampling distributions.

## S2.4 How sensitive are shape estimates to the truncation threshold?

In the `r case1_qsd_sens$n[1]` population-level entries for which shape was estimable under all three thresholds, the shape metric was highly stable to the quasi-stable-distribution truncation rule (Table S14; Figure S4). Relative to the 1% threshold used in the main analysis, the 0.5% threshold changed point estimates by a median absolute amount of `r sprintf('%.3f', case1_qsd_sens$median_abs_diff_pt[case1_qsd_sens$comparison == "0.5% vs 1%"])` and sampling-distribution medians by `r sprintf('%.3f', case1_qsd_sens$median_abs_diff_med[case1_qsd_sens$comparison == "0.5% vs 1%"])`. The more permissive 5% threshold produced somewhat larger but still modest shifts (median absolute changes `r sprintf('%.3f', case1_qsd_sens$median_abs_diff_pt[case1_qsd_sens$comparison == "5% vs 1%"])` and `r sprintf('%.3f', case1_qsd_sens$median_abs_diff_med[case1_qsd_sens$comparison == "5% vs 1%"])`, respectively), with only `r case1_qsd_sens$n_sign_change_pt[case1_qsd_sens$comparison == "5% vs 1%"]` point estimates changing sign relative to the 1% baseline. Those sign changes occurred only for populations whose baseline shape estimates were already very close to zero. Overall, this sensitivity check indicates that the main qualitative results are not driven by the specific 1% truncation threshold.
